   RESPONSE OF NORTHERN VIRGINIA ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. TO
INITIAL BRIEF OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C. AND TO INITIAL BRIEF AND
   JOINT RESPONSES OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS TO
                       PAPER HEARING QUESTIONS

         Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) December 18,

2025 order (“Co-Location Order”),1 Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”)

respectfully submits this response to the initial briefs and joint responses to the paper hearing

questions submitted by PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)2 and the Indicated PJM

Transmission Owners (“PJM Transmission Owners”).3

Interconnection, L.L.C., Notice of Extension of Time, Docket Nos. EL25-49, et al. (issued Jan. 23, 2026) (Accession
No. 20260123-3062) (Extending the due date for responses to initial briefs by seven days, from March 18, 2026, to

  Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, Initial Brief and Joint Responses of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners,

                                                        2
                                           I.      RESPONSE

        A. Introduction and Background

        Co-location in PJM presents contentious issues. An early proposal, based on PJM’s since-

rescinded Guidance on Co-Located Load (“Guidance Document”),4 was filed in Docket No.

ER24-2172 as an amended Interconnection Service Agreement (“ISA”) between Susquehanna

Nuclear LLC, and PPL Electric Utilities Corporation.5 The Commission rejected the Amended

ISA because PJM had not demonstrated a need to deviate from the pro forma ISA.6 Constellation

Energy Generation, LLC (“Constellation”) subsequently filed a complaint to amend PJM’s Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to incorporate the co-location arrangements found in the

Guidance Document.7

        NOVEC is a not-for-profit electric distribution cooperative owned by its members.

NOVEC has significant experience with serving data centers over the past 25 years. NOVEC is

one of the country’s largest data center hubs and serves over 50 data center buildings.8 Based on

its experience, NOVEC opposed Constellation’s complaint in substantial part because

Constellation proposed to relieve the Co-Located Load of any responsibility for transmission

costs, even as that load relied on the transmission system.9 NOVEC is very aware of the potential

effects on cost allocation that can arise because of the size of data centers and does not agree that

data centers or other large loads should be able to use the grid without contributing to its costs.

Guidance Document pending Commission guidance in Docket No. EL25-49.

 The Commission instituted a section 206 show cause proceeding, consolidated the Constellation

complaint with the new show cause proceeding, and directed interested parties to brief a series of

questions regarding whether the PJM Tariff needed to be modified to accommodate co-located

load and, if so, how.10

        The Commission thereafter issued the Co-Location Order on December 18, 2025. The

Co-Location Order found that PJM’s Tariff is not just and reasonable because it does not

“contain provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency the rates, terms, and

conditions of service that apply to generators serving Co-Located Load and Eligible Customers

taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Load.”11 But the Commission included

critical protections for existing transmission customers not present in other previous iterations of

co-location service, including requiring prospective Co-Located Loads to fully fund any network

upgrades before they could take service from an existing generator.12

        In order to facilitate the service of Co-Located Load, the Commission described three

new types of transmission service for Eligible Customers serving Co-Located Load. The

Commission found that additional record evidence was needed to set the appropriate replacement

rates, terms, and conditions of those new types of transmission service, so it set a paper hearing

on eleven questions involving the rates, terms, and conditions of service for Firm Contract

Demand transmission service, Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service, and Interim

Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”).13 PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners

filed initial briefs in response to those questions.14




10
   PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025).
11

                                                      4
        The proposals set forth in the initial briefs strike an appropriate balance between

recognizing the reduced usage of the transmission system for Co-Located Load while also

ensuring that such load does not become a “free rider” to the extent that such load does rely on

and use the transmission system, but does not pay for it. Several important principles should

guide the Commission’s determination of what constitute just and reasonable rates, terms, and

conditions for these new services being mandated to accommodate Co-Located Load. First, the

proposed transmission rates cannot be just and reasonable unless they recover from the Co-

Located Load the full costs associated with the Co-Located Load’s use of and reliance on the

transmission system and do not cause or result in subsidization by existing transmission

customers.

       Second, meaningful financial and operational penalties are necessary. Such penalties

must discourage gamesmanship, must be enforceable, and should include guard-rails such as the

anti-toggling measures proposed by PJM. But penalties should also be tailored to ensure that

they are not written too broadly. As more fully discussed in Section C.4 of these comments, infra

at 14-15, the Commission should direct PJM to modify the penalty provisions to clarify that, in

the event a single Eligible Customer is serving multiple Co-Located Loads, that the

disqualification penalty would only apply to service at the Co-Located Load that disregarded

curtailment instructions or whose transmission protection measures misoperated twice.

       Finally, workable and reliable protections for the transmission system are critical.

Although neither PJM nor the PJM Transmission Owners provided specific criteria yet for the

“special protection schemes” and other necessary controls, the principles they outlined are

sound; the Commission should adopt them.




                                                5
         Notwithstanding the progress that PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners have made in

their proposals, NOVEC respectfully urges the Commission to remain flexible as PJM, the PJM

Transmission Owners, and other Market Participants gain practical experience serving Co-

Located Load. These are entirely new services and may require additional modifications as

experience is gained or as unexpected circumstances arise. As this proceeding advances and

additional details on the proposals become clear, NOVEC reserves the right to oppose the Co-

Location service rates, terms, and conditions if those proposals do not adequately shield existing

transmission customers from subsidizing large-load customers or if they endanger the reliability

of the transmission system.

        B. PJM’s and the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposals to use the NITS rate for
           the new Firm Contract Demand transmission service, Non-Firm Contract
           Demand transmission service, and Interim NITS, impose PJM administrative
           and ancillary service charges, and institute a Grid Reliance Charge are just and
           reasonable, and the Commission should adopt their proposals.

        Above all else, the rates for the new transmission services for the Co-Located Load must

not result in existing transmission customers subsidizing large-load customers. NOVEC supports

the Commission’s acceptance of the proposals of PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners with

respect to rates for Contract Demand transmission service and Interim NITS. NOVEC is

commenting specifically to highlight how critical it is that the proposed rates appropriately

reflect the use of the transmission system by these new services and protect existing transmission

customers from subsidizing Eligible Customers providing transmission service to Co-Located

Load.

               1. Using the NITS rate for Firm Contract Demand transmission service and
                  Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service is appropriate.

        The NITS rate is appropriate in light of the characteristics of Firm Contract Demand

transmission service. Unlike point-to-point service, Contract Demand transmission service is not


                                                 6
 limited to one source, one sink and one path; an Eligible Customer can draw from the

transmission system in a manner comparable to that of a NITS customer. Firm Contract Demand

transmission service is NITS-equivalent, just scaled down to be available for less than the Co-

Located Customers’ total load. Network upgrades still must be planned and constructed as

necessary, with the only difference being that Firm Contract Demand transmission service’s

network upgrades are planned based on contract demand requests instead of anticipated load

growth.15 Because the service otherwise is fundamentally the same, assessing the same

transmission rates as that of NITS makes sense. Because Eligible Customers are receiving a

service commensurate with NITS, they should pay a cost commensurate with NITS in

recognition of the Commission’s cost-causation principles.

        The proposal to charge Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service at the NITS rate

net of the Grid Reliance Charge multiplied by their reserved amount of demand also seems

reasonable. Netting the Grid Reliance Charge prevents double recovery. Like Firm Contract

Demand transmission service, Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service bears a

resemblance to NITS service. Although non-firm, it is a network-type service. In Order No. 888,

the Commission capped non-firm rates at the firm rate.16 Because an Eligible Customer need

only purchase Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service when reserved, transmission

costs for an Eligible Customer are lower than firm rates. Further, as the PJM Transmission

Owners point out, it has a superior priority to non-firm point-to-point transmission service.17 And

because these revenues are credited to the applicable transmission owner’s annual transmission

Utilities, Order No. 888, 75 FERC ¶ 61,080 (1996).

 revenue requirement, this proposal prevents existing load-serving transmission customers from

subsidizing Co-Located Load.

                 2. PJM’s administrative charges are appropriate.

        The Commission asked whether it would be just and reasonable to include charges for

PJM’s administrative services.18 NOVEC agrees with PJM’s proposal to assess administrative

service charges on Co-Located Load.19 These charges are associated with the use of the

transmission system beyond transmission service rates.20 Any entity that uses the transmission

system should contribute to administrative charges associated with the transmission system. The

Commission found that Co-Located Load would use the transmission system even if it did not

draw power from the grid.21 It is thus entirely appropriate for PJM to assess administrative

charges on Co-Located Load. Co-Located Load must bear its fair share of administrative costs.

        The Commission should also accept PJM’s proposal to recover Black Start Service

charges and Regulation charges based on the gross demand of the Co-Located Load for Firm

Contract Demand transmission service and for Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service.

The proposal is consistent with the Commission’s finding “that Eligible Customers taking one of

the new transmission services on behalf of Co-Located Load must be assessed for regulation

service on a gross demand basis at the existing Tariff rate, consistent with the Commission’s

cost-causation principles.”22

                   3. The Commission should accept the Grid Reliance Charge as proposed.

         In the Co-Location Order, the Commission asked whether the rate paid by an Eligible

Customer on behalf of a Co-Located Load that does not reserve any amount of transmission

service should include, besides Regulation and Black Start Services, “an additional charge given

that regulation and black start services could not be provided without the transmission system.”23

The answer to that question is an unequivocal yes. The PJM Transmission Owners have

proposed a Grid Reliance Charge based on the difference between an Eligible Customer’s firm

contract demand (or for Non-Firm Contract Demand customers, the amount of reserved service)

and their gross on-site load.24

         As a threshold matter, Eligible Customers should pay a charge that reflects the need to

deliver these services to their Co-Located Load. Because all other load takes transmission service

up to their gross load, their transmission rates implicitly reflect such use of the transmission

system. The rates of Black Start Service and Regulation do not include a delivery component. If

a Co-Located Load reserved no Firm or Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service, its

payment for those two ancillary services would not include any costs of the transmission system

that are necessary to deliver those services to the Co-Located Load. Without such a charge, the

Co-Located Load would be a free rider on the transmission system, benefiting from the payments

of existing transmission customers to maintain the transmission system without making any

contribution towards it.25




23
   Id. P 219(3).
24
   PJM TO Initial Brief at 14.
25
   Id. at 15 (“Even with a zero MW contract demand, a large Co‑Located Load and generation arrangement will still
depend on the grid for the delivery of various ancillary services and a suite of synchronization support services, such
as stable frequency, inertia, stability services (damping, angle stability), fault current capability, and ride-through
and protection coordination. In short, a Co-Located Load’s net withdrawals do not fully reflect its actual reliance on
the grid.”).

                                                          9
            So, the question becomes whether the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid

Reliance Charge is just and reasonable. There are many possible ways to calculate a Grid

Reliance Charge. The approach has a reasonable foundation, and the Commission should accept

it because the Grid Reliance Charge as proposed is just and reasonable, with an important

distinction: it is limited to depreciation and O&M, conservatively excluding a return on rate base

and associated income taxes. The PJM Transmission Owners only recover their costs and not a

return. Because of the novelty of the Grid Reliance Charge, taking a conservative approach

initially is justifiable. Until PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners gain more experience, the

Grid Reliance Charge is transparent, simple, scales with each utility’s size and cost structure, and

promotes rate stability.26 In the future, the PJM Transmission Owners should explore revising the

methodology to better align the costs of providing access to necessary ancillary services with the

benefits of those services to ensure that Co-Located Load makes an adequate contribution to

those costs. NOVEC views the current proposal as a minimum rate. In addition, because

revenues earned from the Grid Reliance Charge are returned to NITS and Firm Contract Demand

transmission service customers as a revenue credit, the structure avoids any risk of double

recovery. The Commission should accept it as filed by the PJM Transmission Owners. The

Commission may wish to consider ordering PJM to hold a stakeholder process to determine

whether the rate needs to be changed in the future.

           C. PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners are correct that both operational and
              financial penalties are necessary to ensure compliance with rules for Eligible
              Customers serving Co-Located Loads.

           The Commission asked what is the “appropriate penalty charge or other remedial action

that PJM should take to address any unreserved use of the PJM transmission system for an



26
     PJM TO Initial Brief, Ex. PTO-0001 at 24:17-25:14.

                                                          10
 Eligible Customer taking” Firm Contract Demand or Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission

service on behalf of a Co-Located Load.27 PJM proposed three different penalties applicable to

the three transmission services where Eligible Customers: “(i) fail to follow established Load

Shedding and Curtailment procedures; (ii) rely on necessary control technologies or protection

systems in accordance with the PJM Manuals, which may include a RAS, that fail (i.e.,

misoperate) more than once; and (iii) makes unreserved use of the PJM Transmission System.”28

Those penalties are disqualification, a pause in service, and financial penalties.

                 1. Disqualification is appropriate in the circumstances proposed by PJM in
                    order to protect the reliability of the transmission system.

        Disqualification means that an Eligible Customer taking Firm Contract Demand or Non-

Firm Contract Demand transmission service to serve Co-Located Load is disqualified from

taking Firm Contract Demand or Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service for that Co-

Located Load.29 An Eligible Customer disqualified from taking such services for the relevant

Co-Located Load may still take transmission service on behalf of the Co-Located Load by taking

NITS or qualifying for Interim NITS.30 Also, an Eligible Customer taking Interim NITS may be

disqualified from taking service for specific Co-Located Loads, in which case only NITS will be

available once any necessary upgrades are complete.31

        There are two circumstances in which PJM proposes to impose disqualification. First, in

the event that there is a failure to follow Load Shedding or Curtailment procedures for the first

time, the Co-Located Load will be disqualified from receiving Firm Contract Demand

Second, Eligible Customers will be disqualified from taking the contract demand services for the

relevant Co-Located Load upon the second misoperation of necessary control technology and

protection schemes.33

         PJM is responsible for ensuring the provision of reliable electric service to 67 million

people. Not following Load Shedding or Curtailment procedures compromises PJM’s ability to

fulfill its responsibilities. Although PJM has proposed as a compromise allowing one

misoperation of a “special protection scheme” before disqualification, the proposal to disqualify

after repeated misoperations is also necessary to protect the integrity of the transmission system.

Further, NITS remains available to any Co-Located Load that is disqualified from taking the new

services. As PJM explained, the “choice to take NITS, in and of itself, decreases the likelihood of

significant issues arising from failure to curtail, load shed, or misoperation of a necessary control

technology or protection system.”34 Because PJM’s disqualification proposal deters conduct that

threatens the integrity of the transmission system and provides a safe alternative, the

Commission should find it is just and reasonable and adopt it.

                   2. A pause in service is an appropriate compromise for the first
                      misoperation of a necessary control technology or protection system.

         NOVEC supports PJM’s proposal to implement a pause of 120 days from taking

transmission service or withdrawing energy from the transmission system after the first

misoperation of the necessary control technology or protection system.35 Allowing a pause to

 evaluate, investigate, and remedy failures of the necessary control technology is appropriate and

will help develop new procedures and experience to more reliably manage Co-Location.

                  3. Additional financial penalties are warranted.

         NOVEC agrees with PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners that a penalty for

unreserved use in addition to disqualification and pause-in-service rules is appropriate.36 In the

current environment, PJM is correct that “many, if not most, Eligible Customers taking service

on behalf of a Co-Located Load could foreseeably elect to absorb financial penalties for

unreserved use rather than follow Curtailment or Load Shed procedures or avoid misoperation of

the protective technology or system.”37 Financial penalties alone would not be sufficient to

ensure that Co-located Loads and co-located generating facilities comply, through the relevant

Eligible Customers, with their obligations. But that is not sufficient reason to dispense with a

financial penalty.

         A complementary financial penalty should be an additional deterrent that would help

make sure that “the market and other ratepayers are made whole if a Co-Located Load customer

exceeds its contract demand.”38 At this time, neither PJM nor the PJM Transmission Owners

have a specific concept for the Commission to consider, but have committed to working together

to explore penalty options. NOVEC supports those efforts and supports the principle that a

financial penalty should compensate other customers for any harm caused by the Eligible

Customer’s departure from Co-Location requirements or, if there is no harm, that the financial

penalty should be set at a level sufficient to encourage compliance with the PJM Tariff’s

scheduling requirements.

                  4. PJM’s penalty language should be revised to account for conditions
                    where an Eligible Customer serves multiple Co-Located Loads.

        At present, the Illustrative Tariff provides that, when one of the disqualifying events

happens, the Eligible Customer “shall be disqualified from taking Firm Contract Demand

Transmission Service and Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service.”39 PJM has crafted

this language with the assumption that either the generator serving the Co-Located Load or the

Co-Located Load itself would be the Eligible Customer. But the Co-Location Order

contemplates that “any electric utility” could be an Eligible Customer.40 That leaves open the

possibility that the generator, the Co-Located Load, and the Eligible Customer could each be

separate entities. Under those circumstances, the Eligible Customer could reasonably have to rely

upon the Co-Located Load and the co-located generating facility for compliance with curtailment

instructions from PJM and maintenance of equipment to implement the “special protection

schemes.” A third-party Eligible Customer would have limited operational control over the site.

        As drafted, the Illustrative Tariff could result in a third-party Eligible Customer being

disqualified from serving Co-Located Load entirely because of the actions of the Co-Located

Load or the co-located generating facility. This would unreasonably harm the Eligible Customer.

If the Eligible Customer were a Load Serving Entity acting as an Eligible Customer for multiple

Co-Located Loads, it would unreasonably harm those other Co-Located Loads as well.

Accordingly, the Illustrative Tariff should be revised to specify that when a third-party Eligible

Customer is not responsible for a disqualifying event, only the culpable Co-Located Load (and

         D. PJM’s two-pronged approach to implementing an anti-toggling feature for Firm
            Contract Demand transmission service is reasonable and should be accepted.

         The Commission sought comment on the appropriate mechanisms for an anti-toggling

feature for Firm Contract Demand transmission service, including a minimum service period and

minimum notice period.41 The Commission explained that without an anti-toggling feature,

Eligible Customers taking transmission service on behalf of Co-Located Loads “may attempt to

switch between the two new transmission services based on expected capacity market

conditions.”42

         PJM proposed a two-pronged approach. First, Section 709.4 of its Illustrative Tariff

provides that the portion of Co-Located Load served by Firm Contract Demand transmission

service is not eligible to be served by Non-Firm Contract Demand transmission service for “five

years following the effective date of the Service Agreement for Contract Demand Transmission

Service.”43 There is an exception for physical changes to the Co-Located generating facility or

the Co-Located Load that would materially alter the MW-level of power or MW-level of gross

demand.44 The second anti-toggling feature is PJM’s proposed 42-month notice of termination.45

         Both of these proposals are just and reasonable and should be accepted. PJM will have to

procure capacity resources for Firm Contract Demand, and there may be network upgrades

necessary to serve a request for Firm Contract Demand transmission service.46 Setting a

minimum service commitment of five years ensures that timely price signals are sent to the

        E. The Commission should ensure that any “special protection schemes” are robust
           enough to ensure system reliability.

        The Commission asked what interconnection requirements and operational practices are

necessary for “special protection schemes” to maintain system reliability.49 In response, PJM

stated that “[t]he interconnection requirements and operational practices necessary for necessary

control technologies and protection systems to maintain system reliability in the event that a Co-

Located Load or associated generator trips offline will be set forth in the PJM Manuals and, as

applicable, [North American Electric Reliability Corporation] reliability standards.”50 At a

minimum, PJM’s proposal to incorporate North American Electric Reliability Corporation

(“NERC”) reliability standards is just and reasonable.

        The Commission should ensure that there are high reliability standards so that no retail

customers are harmed by the failure of “special protection schemes” of large-load customers.

Retail customers do not have the option to take a lower-quality service to economize. Under no

circumstances should large-load customers choosing a lower-quality service be permitted to

 reduce the reliability of retail customers’ services. The PJM Transmission Owners elucidated

several possible guideposts to consider that would help meet this goal.51

           NOVEC supports those principles. In particular, NOVEC agrees that the “special

protection schemes” should be fully redundant and that the applicable PJM Transmission Owner

should be able to establish technical criteria for the interconnection of Co-Located Load.

Transmission Owners are familiar with the operating characteristics of their own systems, and

any criteria should be flexible enough to include reasonable requirements the Transmission

Owners believe are necessary to protect the transmission system. NOVEC also agrees with the

PJM Transmission Owners that the Commission should direct NERC to establish registration

requirements for Co-Located Loads so that they can be responsible for meeting NERC reliability

standards.

           F. The Commission should approve PJM’s proposed effective date.

           NOVEC agrees with PJM that a reasonable effective date is June 1, 2029. Mr. Horger’s

explanation that it is no longer possible to implement necessary changes to the 2028/2029

Reliability Pricing Model to account for the new transmission services is well-founded.52 The

further explanations that there are necessary software modifications that must be designed and

implemented and that no customers would likely be able to interconnect before then because of

PJM’s interconnection queue further support the June 1, 2029 effective date.

           Besides the impact on PJM, other affected entities must prepare for these new

transmission services to accommodate Co-Located Loads. Any electric utility that may have to

serve a Co-Located Load as an Eligible Customer, or even simply have one in its service

territory, will have to prepare both as an operational matter and consider appropriate regulatory
